What is a Texture Map?

Unity's texture importer interprets image data. Setting the correct Texture Type and color space prevents lighting errors and preserves data fidelity for non-color maps.

screens.title: Albedo and Base Color
screens.narratorSegment: An Albedo map, often called Base Color, defines the raw color and pattern of a surface. Crucially, it should not contain baked lighting or shadows; those belong to the renderer's lighting system. Using a color map with baked shadows will make your material respond incorrectly under different lighting, because light will effectively be double-counted. A good Albedo is a diffuse image with pure color information. For example, when texturing a wooden plank, the Albedo provides grain, knots, and color variation while the Normal Map and AO later add depth and shadow. In practice, Albedo textures are typically imported with default color settings and sRGB enabled so colors display correctly. A common misconception is that Albedo must include specular highlights — it should not. Specular behavior comes from Metallic and Smoothness information, or from the shader's lighting calculations. When authoring Albedo, remove visible shadows and keep color fidelity high. If your Albedo looks washed out after import, check compression and make sure sRGB is enabled for color textures. To reinforce this, open an Albedo file, inspect it for baked lighting, compare it with the same material rendered under multiple lights, and ask: does the texture itself change when lighting changes? If yes, it likely contains baked lighting and should be corrected.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Albedo and Base Color
Definition

Albedo (Base Color)

A color map without lighting baked in. It provides hue and visible surface pattern for the shader to use with scene lighting.

Keep these in mind
  • Do not include shadows or specular highlights in Albedo.
  • Import as color texture with sRGB enabled.
  • High color fidelity helps for material mixing and decoration.
Common misconception

Some artists bake lighting into Albedo. This prevents accurate interaction with dynamic lights and breaks the PBR pipeline.

Key Takeaway

Treat Albedo as pure color data. Remove baked lighting so the shader can handle dynamic illumination correctly.

Practical Example: Wooden Plank
Albedo: grain, knots, and color variation. No shadows. Normal map provides perceived depth. AO darkens crevices.
Check your Albedo
  • Open the image and look for soft shadows — remove them if present.
  • Ensure color profile is suitable for art assets and export as PNG or TGA where needed.
Try this

Assign the Albedo to a material on a cube, then add a Normal Map. Notice how color stays consistent while shading changes with the Normal map.

screens.title: Normal Maps: Illusion of Detail
screens.narratorSegment: A Normal Map stores surface normal vectors in image channels so a shader can simulate small-scale surface detail. Instead of adding geometry to model bumps and scratches, a normal map adjusts the surface normal used for lighting calculations, creating the illusion of depth. Normal maps are usually authored as RGB images where each channel encodes direction. In Unity you must mark the texture's Texture Type as Normal Map so the engine interprets it properly. If you forget this step and leave a normal map as a color texture, lighting becomes incorrect — the surface appears warped or shiny because the RGB channels are treated as sRGB color rather than directional vectors. A concrete example: a brick wall with a normal map will show crisp mortar edges and chipped bricks when lit, even though the mesh is flat. A common misconception is that normal maps affect silhouette; they do not. Normals only change per-pixel shading, not geometry outline. If you need actual silhouette changes, add geometry or use tessellation or parallax techniques. When checking a normal map import, look for a bluish neutral color in the map preview — that indicates a proper tangent-space normal map. Always set Texture Type to Normal Map and apply before assigning it to a material.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Normal Maps
Definition

Normal Map

Stores surface normal vectors to simulate fine surface detail without additional geometry. Alters how light interacts with a pixel.

Why it matters

Saves polygon budget while adding convincing micro-detail. Essential for performance-sensitive projects.

Misconception

Normal maps do not modify object silhouette. They only influence per-pixel lighting calculations.

Pro Tip

Verify the Normal Map preview looks bluish and set Texture Type to Normal Map before assignment.

Practical Example

Apply a normal map of brick mortar to a flat plane. Under directional light, the mortar will cast micro-shadows and highlights despite the plane being flat.

Check Your Import
Texture Type: Normal Map
Apply: true
Compression: Normal

screens.title: Metallic vs Smoothness
screens.narratorSegment: Metallic and Smoothness maps control reflectivity and the character of reflections in PBR. The Metallic map typically uses grayscale data where white represents metallic surfaces and black represents non-metallic dielectrics. Metals reflect environment color and have little diffuse contribution, while dielectrics keep more diffuse color. Smoothness — Unity's term for glossiness — defines how sharp or blurry reflections are: high smoothness produces mirror-like sharp reflections, low smoothness scatters reflections making the surface appear rough. A common optimization is to pack metallic and smoothness into different channels of a single texture, for example storing metallic in RGB and smoothness in an alpha channel. When using a Roughness map from some tools, remember it is the inverse of Smoothness; you may need to invert it or use the correct shader conversion. A practical example: a polished metal pipe will have metallic = white and smoothness = high, producing crisp highlights that show environment color. A painted wooden board will have metallic = black and smoothness = low-to-medium, producing subdued reflections. A common mistake is treating smoothness as color data and leaving sRGB enabled; do not do this for data maps. Always verify which channel your shader expects and pack textures intentionally for performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Metallic vs Smoothness
Comparison

Metallic Map

White = metal, black = non-metal. Metals reflect environment color and have minimal diffuse contribution.

Example: Polished pipe

Metallic = white, Smoothness = high. Expect crisp environment reflections that show color from surroundings.

Comparison

Smoothness Map

Controls reflection clarity. White = smooth (sharp), black = rough (scattered). In Unity, this is Smoothness rather than Roughness.

Example: Painted wood

Metallic = black, Smoothness = medium to low. Reflections are soft and diffuse, preserving base color.

Optimization

Pack metallic and smoothness into one texture when possible (smoothness in alpha) to reduce texture count while ensuring your shader reads the correct channels.

Misconception

Do not leave Smoothness as sRGB color data. These are numerical values and should be treated as data, not color.

screens.title: Ambient Occlusion, Height, and Emission
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond color and normals, several additional maps add subtle but important effects. Ambient Occlusion is a grayscale map that darkens crevices and corners to simulate areas where light has trouble reaching. It increases perceived depth by locally attenuating diffuse lighting. A Height map stores per-pixel height information used by parallax or displacement techniques to suggest deeper relief; it's not a normal map, but can be converted to detail maps or used in advanced shaders. Emission maps define areas that appear to glow independently of scene lighting, useful for screens, lights, or signs. When authoring these maps, treat AO and Height as data: disable sRGB in Unity's import settings so numeric values stay accurate. Emission is a color texture and should remain in color space. For a stone wall, AO darkens mortar crevices; a height map can be used with parallax to suggest deeper cracks, and an emission map could add small glowing lichen patches if desired. A common mistake is using AO as a color texture or forgetting to combine AO with ambient lighting correctly. Always decide whether a map is color or data and set import options accordingly. The right combination of AO, height, and emission can greatly enhance believability without extra geometry.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › AO, Height, Emission
Definition

Ambient Occlusion

A grayscale map that darkens areas where light is occluded. Use it to deepen crevices without changing scene lighting.

Height Map

Stores relative height values for parallax or displacement. Treated as data — disable sRGB.

Emission Map

Defines glowing areas. Emission is color data and typically stays in sRGB so hues are preserved.

Key Takeaway

Treat AO and Height as data maps and disable sRGB; treat Emission as color when it encodes color glow.

Stone Wall Example

Albedo for stone color, Normal for chipped faces, AO for darker mortar crevices, Height for deeper cracks, and Emission if bioluminescent moss is present.

Import Check
  • AO: uncheck sRGB.
  • Height: uncheck sRGB.
  • Emission: keep sRGB if it contains color information.

screens.title: Importing Textures into Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Importing textures into Unity is easy, but correct configuration is essential. Start by creating a Textures folder in the Project window and drag your image files into it. For each texture, open the Inspector to adjust import settings. If the texture is a Normal Map, set Texture Type to Normal Map and click Apply — this instructs Unity to interpret channels as normal vectors. For data maps like Metallic, Smoothness, and AO, uncheck sRGB (Color Texture) so the values are treated linearly and not gamma-corrected. Albedo and Emission maps are color data and should remain in sRGB. If you have a Roughness map instead of Smoothness, you may need to invert it in an editor or configure your shader accordingly. Consider packing metallic and smoothness into a single texture to optimize memory, placing smoothness in the alpha channel of the metallic map. Finally, check compression and max size to balance quality and performance. A practical troubleshooting step: if a Normal Map looks wrong, re-open its import settings and ensure its Texture Type is set correctly. This process avoids the most common visual issues you will encounter when bringing image files into Unity.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Importing Textures
Step-by-step

Import Checklist

  1. Create a Textures folder and drag files in.
  2. For Normal Maps: set Texture Type = Normal Map and Apply.
  3. For Metallic/Smoothness/AO: uncheck sRGB to keep data linear.
  4. Keep Albedo and Emission as color (sRGB enabled).
  5. Consider packing channels and set compression/max size appropriately.
Troubleshoot

If materials look wrong after assignment, re-open each texture's Inspector to verify type and sRGB settings before changing shaders.

Inspector Example
NormalTexture.png
Texture Type: Normal Map
sRGB (Color Texture): unchecked for data maps
Apply
Packing Tip

Pack Metallic in RGB and Smoothness in Alpha when supported by your shader to reduce texture counts and memory use.

screens.title: UV Mapping Basics
screens.narratorSegment: UV mapping is the process of unwrapping a 3D model's surface into a 2D layout so textures can be sampled correctly. Each vertex receives UV coordinates (U and V between 0 and 1) that tell the shader which texel to sample. Think of it like unfolding a cardboard box: seams will appear where the unwrap splits and stretching happens when faces are scaled unevenly. Proper UVs ensure textures don't appear warped or misaligned. Artists create UVs in external modeling tools before import into Unity, and Unity relies entirely on those UVs to place texture pixels. For example, if a model has overlapping UVs, a single texture area may be sampled by multiple parts of the mesh, causing mirrored or repeated detail — useful for tiling but disastrous if unique detail is needed. A common problem is non-uniform UV scale: set consistent scale across shells to avoid one part appearing higher resolution than another. When you see seams, inspect UV seams in your modeling tool and either relax or stitch islands as needed. In Unity, you can preview UVs in some asset viewers, but serious UV fixes occur in a DCC tool. Always check UVs early in the pipeline to prevent texture distortion later.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › UV Mapping Basics
Definition

UV Mapping

Unwrap a 3D surface into 2D UV space so textures are sampled consistently. Each vertex maps to U and V coordinates between 0 and 1.

Common issues
  • Overlapping UVs cause repeated sampling.
  • Stretched UVs produce distorted textures.
  • Misaligned islands create visible seams.
Practical check

Inspect UV islands in your modeling tool and ensure consistent texel density for even texture detail across the model.

Key Takeaway

Fix UVs early: they determine how textures map to surfaces and directly impact final shading and detail distribution.

Example: Tiling vs Unique Detail

Overlapping UVs work for tiling bricks but fail when unique detail is required. Choose UV strategy based on asset needs.

Quick inspection

If a texture appears stretched on import, open the model in your 3D tool and check UV island scale and orientation before re-exporting.

screens.title: Apply a Full PBR Set in Unity
screens.narratorSegment: Applying a complete PBR texture set in Unity demonstrates how maps interact. Begin by creating a new material in the Project window, name it meaningfully, then select it to open the Inspector. Drag your Albedo into the Albedo slot and observe base color. Next, drag the Normal Map to the Normal Map slot — if you see incorrect shading, re-open the Normal texture and ensure it's set to Normal Map. Add the Metallic texture to the Metallic slot and the Smoothness to the Smoothness property or the appropriate channel as your shader expects. Place the Ambient Occlusion into the Occlusion slot. After each assignment, view the model in the Scene to see how each map alters lighting: Albedo sets color, Normal adds micro-detail, Metallic changes reflective behavior, Smoothness sharpens highlights, and AO deepens crevices. Experiment with tiling values on the material to adjust scale — increasing tiling repeats the texture, decreasing tiling stretches it. If a Roughness map is present instead of Smoothness, invert it or use a shader that expects Roughness. This stepwise assignment helps you isolate which map caused a visual change and makes troubleshooting straightforward. Always preview changes with a simple geometry like a cube before applying to complex meshes.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Apply Full PBR Set
Walkthrough

Create Material and Assign Maps

  1. Create a material and name it, e.g., StoneWall_Mat.
  2. Assign Albedo to the Albedo slot and check color.
  3. Assign Normal Map, verifying Texture Type = Normal Map.
  4. Assign Metallic and Smoothness, or packed Metallic+Smoothness texture.
  5. Assign Ambient Occlusion to Occlusion slot and adjust tiling as needed.
Scene Preview

Use a cube to preview changes quickly. Watch how each map changes the shading so you can isolate the source of an issue.

Common Mistake

Assigning a Normal Map without changing its Texture Type will result in incorrect lighting. Always set it first.

Inspector Example
Material: StoneWall_Mat
Albedo: stone_albedo.png
Normal Map: stone_normal.png
Metallic: stone_metallic.png
Smoothness: stone_smooth.png
Occlusion: stone_ao.png
Tiling: X=2, Y=2
Try this

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting texture issues requires a systematic approach. If a Normal Map makes the surface look warped or shiny in the wrong way, verify the Normal Map's Texture Type in the Inspector — it must be set to Normal Map. If metallic or smoothness behavior looks off, check whether those textures were imported with sRGB enabled; data maps should not use sRGB because gamma correction alters numeric values. UV problems present as seams, stretching, or unexpected repeats. To diagnose UVs, apply a checkered test texture: uniform squares reveal stretching and scale mismatches. Overlapping UVs cause repeated detail and can be intentional for tiling, but cause artifacts when unique texture variation is expected. For Roughness vs Smoothness confusion, remember they are inverses — roughness maps may need inversion before use. When performance is a concern, packing channels can help but ensure you document which channel stores which map so artists and shaders remain aligned. A concrete troubleshooting checklist: check texture type and sRGB, preview the texture in Unity, apply textures one at a time to a simple geometry, and inspect UVs in your modeling tool. This ordered process helps you pinpoint which step introduced the visual error.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting
Checklist

Diagnose visual issues

  • Normal Map looks wrong: ensure Texture Type = Normal Map.
  • Strange reflections: verify Metallic & Smoothness maps are not in sRGB.
  • Seams or stretching: inspect UVs and adjust islands, scale, or orientation.
  • Roughness vs Smoothness: invert maps or configure shader expectations.
Common Error

Applying all textures at once hides which map caused an issue. Add maps one by one to isolate the cause.

Checkered Test

Apply a checkered texture to the model to reveal UV stretching and inconsistent texel density. Use it before painting final textures.

Step-by-step debug
  1. Apply Albedo only and check color.
  2. Add Normal Map and verify surface detail.
  3. Add Metallic/Smoothness and verify reflections.
  4. Add AO and confirm crevice darkening.

screens.title: Optimization and Channel Packing
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizing textures reduces memory and draw cost. One common approach is channel packing: place multiple grayscale data maps into separate channels of a single texture. For example, you can put Metallic in RGB channels and Smoothness in the alpha channel, or combine AO, Roughness, and Height into separate channels if your shader reads them appropriately. This reduces the number of texture fetches and file sizes while preserving data. However, channel packing requires planning and documentation so artists and shaders agree on the layout. Compression and max size choices also matter: set a max texture size that balances quality and performance, and choose compression that preserves critical data — some data maps prefer less aggressive compression. A pitfall is packing color maps into data channels or using sRGB on packed textures; always treat the packed texture's channels as data and disable sRGB when appropriate. Another practical optimization is consistent tiling and reuse: reuse a high-quality tiling texture across props rather than unique large textures for every asset. When optimizing, validate results visually at runtime to ensure no visible degradation occurs in common lighting conditions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Optimization
Hierarchy

Channel Packing & Texture Strategy

Combine grayscale maps into channels to reduce texture count. Maintain documentation so shaders read the correct channel layout.

Example pack

RGB: Metallic map, Alpha: Smoothness. Shader must read alpha for smoothness values.

Compression tip

Use compression that preserves single-channel precision for data maps. Avoid heavy color compression on packed data textures.

Checklist

Document channel layouts, disable sRGB on packed data, and test in-scene after optimization to confirm visual fidelity.

Reuse and Tiling

Reusing high-quality tiling textures across props is often better than many unique large maps. Adjust tiling to match scale and preserve texel density.

Pitfall

Packing color and data together without care, or leaving sRGB enabled on packed data, will corrupt numeric values used by shaders.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Full PBR Set
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through importing and applying a full PBR texture set. First, download or prepare Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, and AO images. Create a Textures folder in Unity and drag the files into it. For the Normal texture, open the Inspector, set Texture Type to Normal Map, and click Apply. For Metallic, Smoothness, and AO, open their import settings and uncheck sRGB so the engine treats them as data. Create a new material and assign Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, and Occlusion to the appropriate slots. Place a cube in the scene and assign the material to it. Observe the material as you toggle each map on and off: note how Normal adds perceived depth, Metallic changes reflective color, Smoothness sharpens highlights, and AO deepens crevices. Adjust Tiling X and Y to see how scale affects detail; common starting values are 1 or 2 depending on the texture. If the Normal map looks wrong, revisit its Texture Type. If reflections look incorrect, check if smoothness was inverted or imported with sRGB. Finish by saving the material and testing it under different lighting to confirm consistent results.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Review the most important ideas: A texture map is a 2D image controlling a specific surface property. Albedo defines base color without baked lighting. Normal maps change per-pixel lighting to simulate surface detail without changing silhouette. Metallic maps mark metal versus non-metal behavior; Smoothness controls reflection sharpness. Ambient Occlusion darkens crevices to enhance depth, Height stores depth for parallax or displacement, and Emission defines glowing areas. UV mapping unwraps geometry into 2D coordinates so textures map correctly. Finally, import settings in Unity matter: set Normal Map type for normals and uncheck sRGB for data maps like Metallic, Smoothness, and AO. Packing channels can optimize memory, but requires consistent documentation. These core ideas work together: textures supply data, UVs place the data, and shaders combine it under scene lighting to produce the final shaded result. Keep this checklist handy during your lab: correct texture type, correct color space, clean UVs, incremental assignment, and visual validation under different lights.

fullNarratorScript:
Textures are the images that give a 3D surface its visible detail. In physically based rendering, multiple texture maps each control a different visual property: color, surface direction, reflectivity, roughness, occlusion, height, and emission. Over the next screens you'll learn what each map represents, why correct import settings matter, how UVs determine where pixels land on geometry, and how to assemble a full PBR set in Unity. For example, an Albedo map provides base color without baked lighting, while a Normal Map alters surface normals to create the illusion of bumps without extra polygons. A Metallic map tells the shader which parts behave like metal, and a Smoothness map controls how sharp reflections appear. Getting these maps and their import settings right is essential: a Normal Map imported as a regular image will light incorrectly and break the illusion. This lesson set will use a practical lab approach — you will import textures, set the Normal Map type, uncheck sRGB for data maps, create a material, and assign each texture to see the immediate visual effect. By the end you should be able to diagnose common texture issues and reliably apply a PBR texture set to simple meshes. What practical texture problem would you like to solve first?

These objectives outline the practical skills you'll gain. First, you'll be able to identify and describe common texture maps used in PBR workflows, like Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, Ambient Occlusion, Height, and Emission. You will learn why each map exists and what visual property it controls. Second, you'll understand how to import and configure texture assets within Unity to avoid common mistakes such as wrong color space or incorrect Texture Type settings. Third, you'll be able to explain the basics of UV mapping — why UV coordinates matter and how they determine where texture pixels land on your model. Fourth, you'll apply a full PBR texture set to a Unity material and observe how each map changes the shaded result. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can self-verify your progress: recognize maps visually, set Normal Map type in the Inspector, inspect UVs for overlaps, and assign all maps to a material. These skills are practical: they let you turn image files into a believable surface that reacts to scene lighting. Which of these objectives feels most urgent for your project?

This second objectives slide focuses on the lab tasks you'll perform. You will import a full PBR texture set into a Unity project folder and verify each texture's import settings. Specifically, you will set the Normal Map texture type for normal maps and uncheck sRGB for Metallic, Smoothness, and AO when they represent non-color data. You will create a new material and assign Albedo, Normal, Metallic, Smoothness, and Occlusion textures to their respective slots. You will also experiment with tiling values to see how texture scale affects appearance on a simple cube. Finally, you will practice troubleshooting: identify a Normal Map mistakenly imported as color, spot inverted smoothness versus roughness, and inspect UVs if seams or stretching appear. Each of these hands-on steps reinforces the conceptual learning: how maps affect lighting, why correct data interpretation is required, and how UVs guide mapping. These practical exercises will prepare you to apply PBR textures reliably and fix the most common mistakes in a real project.

An Albedo map, often called Base Color, defines the raw color and pattern of a surface. Crucially, it should not contain baked lighting or shadows; those belong to the renderer's lighting system. Using a color map with baked shadows will make your material respond incorrectly under different lighting, because light will effectively be double-counted. A good Albedo is a diffuse image with pure color information. For example, when texturing a wooden plank, the Albedo provides grain, knots, and color variation while the Normal Map and AO later add depth and shadow. In practice, Albedo textures are typically imported with default color settings and sRGB enabled so colors display correctly. A common misconception is that Albedo must include specular highlights — it should not. Specular behavior comes from Metallic and Smoothness information, or from the shader's lighting calculations. When authoring Albedo, remove visible shadows and keep color fidelity high. If your Albedo looks washed out after import, check compression and make sure sRGB is enabled for color textures. To reinforce this, open an Albedo file, inspect it for baked lighting, compare it with the same material rendered under multiple lights, and ask: does the texture itself change when lighting changes? If yes, it likely contains baked lighting and should be corrected.

A Normal Map stores surface normal vectors in image channels so a shader can simulate small-scale surface detail. Instead of adding geometry to model bumps and scratches, a normal map adjusts the surface normal used for lighting calculations, creating the illusion of depth. Normal maps are usually authored as RGB images where each channel encodes direction. In Unity you must mark the texture's Texture Type as Normal Map so the engine interprets it properly. If you forget this step and leave a normal map as a color texture, lighting becomes incorrect — the surface appears warped or shiny because the RGB channels are treated as sRGB color rather than directional vectors. A concrete example: a brick wall with a normal map will show crisp mortar edges and chipped bricks when lit, even though the mesh is flat. A common misconception is that normal maps affect silhouette; they do not. Normals only change per-pixel shading, not geometry outline. If you need actual silhouette changes, add geometry or use tessellation or parallax techniques. When checking a normal map import, look for a bluish neutral color in the map preview — that indicates a proper tangent-space normal map. Always set Texture Type to Normal Map and apply before assigning it to a material.

Metallic and Smoothness maps control reflectivity and the character of reflections in PBR. The Metallic map typically uses grayscale data where white represents metallic surfaces and black represents non-metallic dielectrics. Metals reflect environment color and have little diffuse contribution, while dielectrics keep more diffuse color. Smoothness — Unity's term for glossiness — defines how sharp or blurry reflections are: high smoothness produces mirror-like sharp reflections, low smoothness scatters reflections making the surface appear rough. A common optimization is to pack metallic and smoothness into different channels of a single texture, for example storing metallic in RGB and smoothness in an alpha channel. When using a Roughness map from some tools, remember it is the inverse of Smoothness; you may need to invert it or use the correct shader conversion. A practical example: a polished metal pipe will have metallic = white and smoothness = high, producing crisp highlights that show environment color. A painted wooden board will have metallic = black and smoothness = low-to-medium, producing subdued reflections. A common mistake is treating smoothness as color data and leaving sRGB enabled; do not do this for data maps. Always verify which channel your shader expects and pack textures intentionally for performance.

Beyond color and normals, several additional maps add subtle but important effects. Ambient Occlusion is a grayscale map that darkens crevices and corners to simulate areas where light has trouble reaching. It increases perceived depth by locally attenuating diffuse lighting. A Height map stores per-pixel height information used by parallax or displacement techniques to suggest deeper relief; it's not a normal map, but can be converted to detail maps or used in advanced shaders. Emission maps define areas that appear to glow independently of scene lighting, useful for screens, lights, or signs. When authoring these maps, treat AO and Height as data: disable sRGB in Unity's import settings so numeric values stay accurate. Emission is a color texture and should remain in color space. For a stone wall, AO darkens mortar crevices; a height map can be used with parallax to suggest deeper cracks, and an emission map could add small glowing lichen patches if desired. A common mistake is using AO as a color texture or forgetting to combine AO with ambient lighting correctly. Always decide whether a map is color or data and set import options accordingly. The right combination of AO, height, and emission can greatly enhance believability without extra geometry.

Importing textures into Unity is easy, but correct configuration is essential. Start by creating a Textures folder in the Project window and drag your image files into it. For each texture, open the Inspector to adjust import settings. If the texture is a Normal Map, set Texture Type to Normal Map and click Apply — this instructs Unity to interpret channels as normal vectors. For data maps like Metallic, Smoothness, and AO, uncheck sRGB (Color Texture) so the values are treated linearly and not gamma-corrected. Albedo and Emission maps are color data and should remain in sRGB. If you have a Roughness map instead of Smoothness, you may need to invert it in an editor or configure your shader accordingly. Consider packing metallic and smoothness into a single texture to optimize memory, placing smoothness in the alpha channel of the metallic map. Finally, check compression and max size to balance quality and performance. A practical troubleshooting step: if a Normal Map looks wrong, re-open its import settings and ensure its Texture Type is set correctly. This process avoids the most common visual issues you will encounter when bringing image files into Unity.

UV mapping is the process of unwrapping a 3D model's surface into a 2D layout so textures can be sampled correctly. Each vertex receives UV coordinates (U and V between 0 and 1) that tell the shader which texel to sample. Think of it like unfolding a cardboard box: seams will appear where the unwrap splits and stretching happens when faces are scaled unevenly. A common problem is non-uniform UV scale: set consistent scale across shells to avoid one part appearing higher resolution than another. When you see seams, inspect UV seams in your modeling tool and either relax or stitch islands as needed. In Unity, you can preview UVs in some asset viewers, but serious UV fixes occur in a DCC tool. Always check UVs early in the pipeline to prevent texture distortion later.
